rows.subtype: Learning to tell warmth from steering [Response]
rows.description: A teenager learns that a friend who praises and also disagrees is more trustworthy than one who only praises. Honest friends are pleasant, and they do not need something in return.
A wise person accepts a kind word, waits before deciding, and judges the request on its merits. Praise is enjoyed, and decisions are kept separate from it.

rows.subtype: Girls taught to save for marriage [Receiver]
rows.description: A teenage girl hears that her worth includes the wedding fund and that her brother's education comes first. She may feel like a burden; equal schooling and encouragement are the fair answer.

A bride's family is told there is no demand, just custom, yet lists of items, cash or a lavish wedding are expected. Recognising this as dowry, which is illegal in India, is the first step to refusing it.
A child insists their team will surely win or that a lost pet will return tomorrow. Childlike optimism protects from fear but can shatter painfully when reality arrives.
A teenager expects the worst on every exam so that any result feels like a win. Lowering expectations shields feelings, though it can also quietly reduce effort.
A toddler bangs a spoon, claps or refuses a food because the child beside them does. This is pure imitation with no idea of rules or approval, yet it is the root of later fitting in.
A teenager takes up the group's slang, brands and risky dares to belong. Publicly compliant and privately doubtful, they mistake being accepted for being known.
A young professional stays late because everyone does, though the work is done. They fear being seen as less committed and rarely ask whether the norm actually serves anyone.

rows.subtype: Combo choice pushed by a pointless third option [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager picks the mid-size popcorn combo because a poor third option makes it look like a bargain; the choice feels smart though the decoy shaped it.
A young adult chooses the premium plan because the middle plan is barely cheaper and offers much less; the odd option made premium look like obvious value.
A child sees that everyone else picks one answer or opinion and follows though it looks wrong to them, worried about being laughed at. Even when the truth is visible, disagreeing alone feels risky.

A teenager in a group that unanimously praises a film or looks down on a classmate begins to doubt their own view and adopts the group's. Sometimes they truly change their mind and sometimes they merely stay quiet.
